title: COLD OPEN
paras: Eleven and a half thousand years ago, on a limestone hill in what is now southeastern Turkey, people carved stone pillars taller than a man, some of them weighing around ten tonnes.
They had no metal. No wheel. No writing. No pottery. They did not farm. They lived by hunting wild animals and gathering wild plants.

And yet they raised great rings of carved stone, decorated with foxes, snakes, boars and vultures. Then, over many centuries, the rings were filled with earth, and the hill kept its secret for ten thousand years.
Today we call it Gobekli Tepe. Potbelly Hill.

title: TITLE
paras: In this documentary, we'll go back to the end of the last Ice Age and stand inside these stone circles as they were being built. And we'll try to answer three questions. Who could build something like this before farming existed? What were these enclosures for? And why did the world forget them?

title: DISCOVERY
paras: In nineteen sixty-three, a team from Istanbul University and the University of Chicago walked across the hills around the city of Sanliurfa, recording ancient sites. On one rounded hill, about fifteen kilometres from the city, they noticed thousands of flint flakes lying on the ground, and some broken slabs of limestone.
The hill had a lone mulberry tree on top, and a few graves. The surveyors thought the slabs might be gravestones from a medieval cemetery. They wrote a short note, and moved on.
For thirty years, almost nobody looked again. Farmers ploughed the slopes, and now and then their ploughs struck large stones, which they dragged to the edges of their fields.

In nineteen ninety-four, a German archaeologist named Klaus Schmidt read that old survey report. Schmidt had spent years excavating at Nevali Chori, a site not far away, where people of the Stone Age had built a cult building with T-shaped stone pillars. That site was later flooded by the reservoir of the Ataturk Dam. When Schmidt read about broken limestone slabs on a hill covered in flint, he suspected they were not gravestones at all.

He was right. The slabs were the tops of enormous T-shaped pillars, still standing in the ground. In nineteen ninety-five, excavations began, run by the German Archaeological Institute together with the Sanliurfa Museum.

As the digging went deeper, the scale became clear. The mound was about fifteen metres high and around three hundred metres across. And it was not a natural hill. Much of it was made by people, from stone, earth, rubble and the remains of their activity, built up over more than a thousand years.
Inside it were round and oval enclosures, ten to thirty metres across. Each was ringed by stone walls and pillars facing inwards, and in the centre of each stood two huge pillars, side by side.

Then came the dates. Radiocarbon tests showed that the oldest enclosures were built around eleven and a half thousand years ago. That is roughly six thousand years before Stonehenge, and seven thousand years before the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Schmidt summed up what he believed the site meant in a single line. First came the temple, then the city.

title: THE WORLD AFTER THE ICE
paras: To understand why that was such a shock, we need to picture the world these people lived in.

Around twelve thousand years ago, the last Ice Age was finally ending. After a sudden cold spell that lasted more than a thousand years, the climate warmed quickly. Rain returned to the hills of the Near East. Grasslands spread. Wild wheat and barley grew in thick stands on the slopes, and great herds of gazelle moved across the plains.

The people here were hunter-gatherers. They hunted gazelle, wild cattle called aurochs, wild boar, red deer and wild asses. They gathered wild cereals, lentils, almonds and pistachios. Their tools were made of flint, bone and wood.

For most of human history, the standard view was simple. First, people learned to farm. Farming produced surplus food. Surplus food allowed villages, then towns, then specialists, priests and rulers. And only then, much later, could a society organise the labour to build monuments.
Gobekli Tepe seemed to turn that order upside down. Here were monuments, built by people who had not yet domesticated a single plant or animal.

And it was not alone. Across the same region, archaeologists have since found a whole family of similar sites, with T-shaped pillars, carved animals and round buildings. Since twenty twenty-one, Turkish researchers have been studying more than a dozen of them in a project called Tas Tepeler, the Stone Hills.
At one of them, Karahan Tepe, excavators found a room carved directly into the bedrock, with a row of stone pillars and a human head sculpted so that it seems to emerge from the wall.
So Gobekli Tepe was not a one-off miracle. It was the most famous part of a whole culture, one that existed in these hills at the very dawn of the farming age.

title: RE-HOOK
paras: But a name and a date don't tell us what it felt like to stand inside these circles. So let's step into the largest enclosure that has been excavated, and look at what is carved on the stones. Because some of these carvings are among the strangest images ever made by human hands.

title: THE PILLARS
paras: Archaeologists label the main enclosures with letters, A to D. The most impressive is Enclosure D, around twenty metres across.
At its centre stand two pillars, numbered eighteen and thirty-one. Each is about five and a half metres tall, carved from a single block of limestone.

At first they look like simple stone shapes. Then you notice the arms. Carved in low relief down the sides of each pillar are human arms, bent at the elbow, with long fingers that meet at the front, just above a belt. Below the belt hangs what looks like a loincloth made of fox pelts.

The T-shape, it turns out, is a body. The top of the T is the head. The pillar is a stylised human figure, or perhaps something more than human. They have no faces. Whether they represent ancestors, spirits or gods, we do not know.
Around them, in the enclosure wall, stand smaller pillars, and these are covered in animals.

There are foxes with bared teeth. Wild boars. Snakes that run down the stone in long lines. Cranes, ducks, and wild cattle with sweeping horns. Scorpions, and big cats that may be lions, or perhaps leopards. On one pillar in Enclosure A, a bull, a fox and a crane are carved one above the other.

Most of the animals are dangerous ones. Predators, poisonous creatures, scavengers. These are not simply pictures of dinner. The gazelle, which these people hunted more than any other animal, is rarely shown at all.

The most famous carving is on Pillar forty-three, now known as the Vulture Stone. A large vulture spreads its wings, with a round object near one wing. Around it are other birds, a scorpion, and near the bottom, a figure that appears to be a man without a head.

In the Stone Age Near East, vultures are often linked with death. Some archaeologists think the Vulture Stone shows a funeral rite, in which the dead were left in the open for birds to clean the bones. Others read it as a myth, or the symbol of a group. The truth is, the image is powerful, and its meaning is still open.

There were also sculptures in the round. A boar. Carved heads. And in twenty twenty-three, researchers announced a life-size statue of a wild boar from Gobekli Tepe with traces of red, black and white pigment still on it. It is a reminder that this place may once have been far more colourful than the bare grey stone we see today.
How were these pillars made? The answer lies in the bedrock around the hill. Archaeologists have found the quarries, where pillars were cut directly from the limestone plateau using flint tools.

One pillar was never finished. It still lies in the quarry, almost seven metres long, partly separated from the rock. Had it been completed and moved, it would have been one of the largest pillars on the site.

Cutting it would have taken weeks of hammering with stone. Moving it would have needed ropes, wooden levers, sledges, and a large number of people working together. And then the carving, done by someone who knew exactly what the animals should look like, and where each one belonged.

This is the real mystery of Gobekli Tepe. Not that the stones were impossible to move. They weren't. But that people with no farms, no towns and no kings decided to do it, again and again, over centuries.

title: WHO BUILT IT, AND WHY
paras: For many years, the most popular answer was Klaus Schmidt's. He saw Gobekli Tepe as a sanctuary on a hill, a meeting place for scattered bands of hunter-gatherers who came together for rituals, but did not live there.

In his view, the effort of building it pushed people towards farming. To feed hundreds of workers and guests, they needed more food in one place. Wild cereals were harvested more and more intensively, and slowly the plants began to change.

There is a striking clue nearby. Genetic studies of modern einkorn wheat, one of the very first domesticated crops, point to the Karacadag mountains, not far from Gobekli Tepe, as one of the places where it was first domesticated. The idea that religion came first and farming followed became one of the most famous ideas in modern archaeology.

But research did not stop when Schmidt died in twenty fourteen. A new team, led by archaeologist Lee Clare of the German Archaeological Institute, kept digging, and the picture has become more complicated.

They found smaller rectangular buildings that look like houses. They found thousands of grinding stones used to process cereals and other plants, far more than a few festivals would need. They found cisterns cut into the bedrock to collect rainwater, and channels leading water across the hill.

In other words, people may have lived here, at least part of the time. Gobekli Tepe may have been both a settlement and a ritual centre, a place where daily life and ceremony were mixed together, as they are in many traditional societies.

What we know for certain is that people ate here, in large numbers. Excavators have found huge quantities of animal bones, especially gazelle, along with aurochs and wild boar. Many of them were broken open to get at the marrow. It looks like the remains of feasting.
Some researchers have even suggested that cereals were brewed into a kind of beer, using large limestone vessels found at the site. That idea is attractive, but the evidence is still debated.

Feasting matters, because it may be the key to how the work was organised. In many societies without money or rulers, people come together for big projects because someone provides food and drink, and because the gathering itself has meaning. A shared feast can turn strangers into a community.

There is one more find that hints at a darker side of ritual. Among the bones, researchers found fragments of human skulls with deep grooves carved into them, made after death. A hole was drilled in at least one of them, perhaps so the skull could be hung up and displayed.

Skull rituals are known from other Stone Age sites in the Near East, where the dead were often buried under houses and their skulls later removed and treated with care. At Gobekli Tepe, the carved skulls may have been honoured ancestors. Or something else entirely.

The people who built Gobekli Tepe were also connected to a wider world. Among the flint tools are a few blades of obsidian, a volcanic glass, which came from sources hundreds of kilometres away. Ideas, materials and perhaps people were moving across the region.

So who built Gobekli Tepe? Not a lost civilization, and not slaves under a king. The best evidence points to local communities of hunter-gatherers, living at a turning point in human history, who chose to work together on something that mattered to them more than anything else.

title: THE BURIAL
paras: Over time, Gobekli Tepe changed. The oldest enclosures, the great round rings with the giant pillars, belong to the earliest phase. In later centuries, people built smaller rectangular rooms, with shorter pillars and fewer carvings.
And at some point, the great enclosures were filled in. Stone, rubble, flint, bone, earth. The space between the pillars disappeared beneath it.

Klaus Schmidt believed this was done on purpose, that people deliberately buried their monuments, perhaps as a final ritual when an enclosure was no longer used. It is a dramatic idea, and it helped make Gobekli Tepe famous.

Newer studies suggest a slower and messier story. Some of the fill may have come from slopes sliding into the enclosures, after which people repaired walls, propped up pillars and rebuilt inside them, more than once. Some filling may well have been deliberate. Archaeologists are still working out the details.

Either way, by around ten thousand years ago, the site had been abandoned. By then, farming villages were spreading across the Near East. People were herding sheep and goats, growing domesticated wheat and barley, and living in permanent houses. The world that built Gobekli Tepe had moved on.
The hill sat quietly for thousands of years. Empires rose and fell around it. And it waited, until a survey team in nineteen sixty-three mistook its pillars for gravestones.

title: WHAT WE KNOW VS. WHAT WE DON'T
paras: So let's separate what we know, from what we don't.

We know that the earliest enclosures were built around eleven and a half thousand years ago. We know they were built with stone tools, by people who did not farm. And we know the T-shaped pillars represent stylised human figures.
We know the site was used and rebuilt for more than a thousand years. And we know it belonged to a wider culture, with many similar sites across the region.

What we don't know is what the builders believed. We don't know who or what the central pillars represent. We don't know exactly what the enclosures were used for, or why the great rings were filled in.

And there is one more thing we should be clear about. Gobekli Tepe is often used as evidence for a lost advanced civilization, or for a comet that the builders supposedly recorded on the Vulture Stone. Archaeologists do not accept these claims. There are no metal tools, no writing, no farmed crops and no machinery at the site. What there is, is thousands of flint tools, animal bones, and the work of human hands.

Geophysical surveys suggest that at least twenty enclosures still lie beneath the mound, and only a small part of the site has been excavated. Since twenty eighteen, Gobekli Tepe has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Some of its biggest answers may still be underground.

And perhaps that is the real lesson of this place. The people of the Ice Age were not simple. Long before cities, kings and writing, they could plan, organise and create on a monumental scale. They were people like us, with the same minds, trying to make sense of a dangerous and beautiful world.

title: OUTRO
paras: Eleven and a half thousand years ago, hunters on a hill in Anatolia carved their world into stone. Foxes and vultures, snakes and boars, and silent figures with arms folded across their bodies.

We may never know their names, their language or their gods. But they left us some of the oldest monumental art ever found, and the clearest proof that human imagination is older than civilization itself.

If you want to see what came seven thousand years later, watch our documentary on Mohenjo-daro, the lost city of the Indus, on screen now. And if you enjoyed this journey, subscribe to Ashen Atlas. Thanks for watching.
